text: This study of cities fails to reflect reality, according to book reviewer Ted Searle

text: With Leon Holbrook's 'We Should Live In Cities' you are definitely getting seventeen pounds worth of book; £17, and possibly somewhere approaching 17lbs as well, because this is a hefty tome, not lavish enough for the coffee table, but not entirely comfortable to read in bed. Which raises the question, what audience exactly is it aimed at? People who see the city as a fundamental achievement in human development, or those for whom urbanism is just another trend? Recently the world reached a tipping point, with more people living in cities than ever before, and this is reflected in contemporary culture: there are increasing numbers of books, films and TV programmes about the 'city'.

text: In some respects, Holbrook's is a reasonably efficient addition to the genre. He does provide a comprehensive overview of the state of cities as they are today, and contemporary thinking in urbanism. However, when it comes to the development of cities over the centuries, his account is more biased and selective.

text: At its best the book resembles a collection of feature articles on contemporary cities. Holbrook provides a detailed and readable account of public transport in South America, and the economics of Mumbai's infamous Dharavi – a slum that is exposed as a complex and curiously efficient neighbourhood. He also covers Chinese urbanisation well, carefully describing the system of residential registration that allows for the ever-accelerating migration from the countryside. Holbrook is at pains to retain a global perspective, writing more about the cities of the emergent BRIC economies – the economies of Brazil, Russia, India and China – than he does about established old world cities in Europe. He rightly sees the future of the city as being shaped by developments in the East and the South, where the cities of the 21st century will arise.

text: But at its worst 'We Should Live In Cities' is a pretty inferior piece of work: a mixture of extreme blind optimism and unimaginative theories stitched together by cliche. Does it matter that in a book about cities the author uses such expressions – quite without irony – as 'vibrant art scene'? Well, yes, I think it does. But then this is a writer who will never use the expression 'low tax' when he instead can reach for a euphemism like 'light touch fiscal policy'. To seriously tackle his awkwardness of expression would place someone in the unenviable position of deciding how much should be changed because, in fact, so much needs to be changed.

text: I think the problem with 'We Should Live In Cities' derives from its title. It does not matter whether the emphasis is placed on 'should' or not, the end result is that the reader feels rather intimidated. Try telling the single mother or father with children who has just had to leave London because of rising living costs that cities are good for them; or why not convey the advantages of a vibrant art scene to the people who live in the shanty towns of Lagos and Johannesburg, or the slums of Jakarta and Dhaka? Even disregarding financial issues there are still those of us who experience a sense of profound isolation from the city on a daily basis – from its congestion, its chilly depersonalization, and its eagerness to reduce support for the community – an alienation that we still feel ambivalent about, loving and hating it as we love the cities that produce such powerful feelings.

text: It is not that Holbrook does not acknowledge the downside of cities - he includes a section about how violence is already a feature of many contemporary urban centres, and is not unsympathetic to those who are dissatisfied with these places. Nor does he ignore the implication that widening inequality may become an unavoidable problem of larger and larger cities. Yet Holbrook says that for the city to remain good for us it must address problems such as sustainability and trust. He acknowledges that the cure for the increasing urban problems cannot be found in the current market, and yet he offers no real alternative.

text: Then there is the built environment; for someone prepared to spend 400 pages telling us how great cities are, Holbrook seems remarkably untouched by the physical structure and beauty of buildings. Say what you will about the European designer Le Corbusier – considered the father of modern architecture – he did know how to design an elegant building; and his modernism was a genuine response to the technology of the time. I tend to think of cities first and foremost in this visually appealing way, even if urban planners do not.

text: In truth, the real problem in the city of London, where Mr Holbrook and I live, is financial – the absurd tax system and the problem this creates for a true local democracy. It is an issue that has destroyed the system that in the past once made London a livable city for people of all classes. I do not imagine these financial developments – taking place in cities all over the world – will be good for you, no matter how glossy this handsomely produced book makes them look.
